rv.q: Noises Off remains as reliable an engine of joy as there is on the British stage.
Now 40 years old, the play has lost little of its dizzy joy or deep poignancy.
Mostly Noises Off is just blissfully, brilliantly funny.
This is a superior revival to the one seen in 2019, with a sense – spurred by the pandemic? – of top-rank stage-actors relishing the deranging peculiarity of their profession.
With a script as precision-honed as this, waves of laughter are inevitable and unstoppable.
Acts I and III, featuring events front of stage, are mildly amusing. Act II, when we see the panic and calamities backstage, can be the stuff of genius.

Basically, ‘Noises Off’ is both timeless and dated and I honestly think that it’s a rare play that would probably benefit from a straight-up modern remake (one that goes beyond bland tribute act ‘The Play That Goes Wrong’).
Solidly entertaining, then; it just doesn’t take your breath away.
The entire thing breezes away the January blues with glorious brilliance.
The fantastically farcical fishy goings-on at this show-within-a-show make for a ferociously funny evening.
Anarchy has never seemed so sublime.

It’s still very satisfying to see the middle section from a backstage perspective, emotions boiling over in near silence (the noises off must be contained after all) as who doesn’t enjoy a bit of meta these days?

cn.t: Frayn's beloved farce-within-a-farce remains a reliably hilarious crowd-pleaser in this 40th anniversary revival, with critics praising its meticulous plotting and the chaotic brilliance of Act II, though some find the timing less sharp than ideal.
